name: Carlos Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play percussion for a civic orchestra, record short rhythm parts and teach four pupils. I have a music bachelor’s and enough seasons to check the drum inventory and lead a section rehearsal, though I am a working player rather than a star. I like the moment the whole hall comes in together; I dislike finding a written fee that leaves setup time out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much room do you have at home to change course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works in the transit office and our children are grown and away. We have a small mortgage and ten months of bills saved; orchestra and recording fees are high for this job, and several ensembles hire nearby. I have never used AI tools and still go through the instrument log with a colleague by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that a faster booking sheet is fine if it still shows paid setup and rehearsal hours. I would ask the section to check the instrument log together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra season, four pupils and my partner’s transit wage cover the mortgage. Ten months saved absorbs an ordinary cancelled concert, with other venues nearby if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid orchestra dates, recordings and four pupils, and get the next run’s setup and cancellation fees in writing. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension estimate before setting any retirement date and save one fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our present income. A signed setup hour is work, even when no audience hears it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the instrument log cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check each drum and stand before a call and tell the stage crew what needs repair. An unchecked stand can end a rehearsal fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have no actual pension figure yet. My partner and I would compare the estimate with our bills before setting any date.

I would check the **instrument log** with the section.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** covers an ordinary cancelled concert without forcing a missed mortgage payment.
Current **orchestra and transit wages** cover the mortgage through this booked season.
do: Keep **orchestra, recordings and pupils** with written setup and cancellation fees.
Request **actual pension estimate**; save fifth of cleared extra recordings after essentials toward twelve months.
feel: I feel **calm** about paid work and near-term bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the musicians’ union which recording and setup hours remain paid. A live drum section still has people lifting and checking every stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect short advert rhythms to lose buyers and perhaps one paid setup call to go. Those fees are about a quarter of my pay, and ten months saved cannot turn a lost contract into income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would bring the last two seasons of setup hours to the union and seek a written minimum, while keeping orchestra and four pupils. If two monthly advert calls disappear, I would seek a posted paid instrument-steward role only if my music bachelor’s and drum-inventory experience meet its requirements, it still pays for actual hands-on inspection, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the route works; I would keep music until a signed offer during disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real part of my income shrinking. The reserve gives us time to argue and apply, not a licence to ignore a missing fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union take to management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee sheets and the hours spent moving drums before a rehearsal. I would want a written rate for setup, not applause for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI instrument log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and I still want a person to check the stand and sign the repair line. A tidy screen cannot test a loose clamp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that 2028 thinking AGI could book and make rhythm tracks before robot drummers arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed paid dates and setup hours now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect advert calls to end and some paid orchestra setup hours to shrink in 2028. That would cut a noticeable part of my own pay, though live concerts may still need players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get signed orchestra dates and setup terms and keep four pupils. In the first year after 2028, if adverts end and setup hours fall, I would apply for a posted paid instrument-steward role only if my music bachelor’s and drum-inventory experience qualify, the post pays actual hands-on checks, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and transport works; I would keep orchestra and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the pay cut, not trapped. Ten months saved and several local employers let me check actual openings, not assume one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the steward job be just software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read its paid duties. If a machine handles only bookings, someone still has to inspect a drum safely. I need paid hands-on drum inspections listed in the steward job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When do robots matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Capable robot drummers are around 2031 in this card. Recording and booking fees could change in 2028, so the first contract check comes earlier.

transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that five years is time to put setup and recorded-use fees into the orchestra agreement. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot drummers around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert rhythms may lose buyers before live playing does. I could test a separate adult drum circle. Our mortgage reserve should not pay a drum circle's room deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid orchestra and four pupils and get the hall room and hire charge agreed in writing before taking deposits, outside my booked calls. If two monthly advert fees disappear, I would start a separate six-week adult drum circle only after ten deposits cover my teaching and preparation, a paid setup assistant, room hire, safe drum rental and travel; I would replace an unsafe drum or defer and refund the whole group below ten safe paid places, repeating after 2031 only with the same full wages and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording income over the next few years. Five years gives me time to check real paid seats without taking money from the mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only eight adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would return all eight deposits and defer the date. Ten are needed to pay the assistant, room and my preparation without using savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a hired drum is unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would find a safe replacement first. If I cannot keep ten safe paid places, I would defer and refund the whole group, not short anyone’s wage.

transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot drummers around 2039 are different dates. I would still ask who gets paid for setup today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might want fewer evening concerts, but I have no retirement date without the actual pension estimate. Ten months saved and current orchestra and transit wages secure the next few years, though not every year after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep orchestra and four pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save one fifth of cleared extra drum-circle surplus after my teaching/preparation, assistant, room, safe hire, travel, mortgage and food toward twelve months. Across the decade I would run the separate circle outside booked orchestra calls only after room booking and hire charge are agreed in writing before deposits; ten fees then cover those wages and costs, replacing unsafe drums or deferring and refunding the whole group below ten safe paid places; in the first year after 2036 I would repeat only on that full paid floor and keep orchestra dates that still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recording fees while current work meets the mortgage. A decade helps us set terms, not count future deposits as wages.

transcript.text: Would you buy ten drums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would rent safe ones only against ten paid places and keep the reserve for bills. A failed drum gets replaced or the whole group is deferred and refunded below ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not set that date. I would read the actual pension estimate with our bills and available paid work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because adverts and setup fees could fall before a posted paid steward role appears. Signed orchestra dates, a real role paying for hands-on checks and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tightens the loose drum stand before the first note. A neat instrument log cannot hold up a falling drum.

headlineQuote: A neat instrument log cannot hold up a falling drum.
portrait: Carlos is an **experienced percussionist** with a music bachelor’s, four pupils and higher music pay.
He has **ten months saved**, a transit-office partner, grown children and a mortgage.
He has **never used AI** and brings written setup-hour records to his union.
His **separate drum circle** needs ten safe paid places, written room hire and full wages outside orchestra calls.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut advert and setup fees before a real paid steward post appears.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **signed orchestra dates**, a paid human inspection role and written replacement net after travel.
